title: Tantalus and his torture
subtitle: Close, never close enough
subject: mythologie
description: Tantalus serves her son to the gods. His punishment: water and fruit always out of reach. A myth of frustration that even named a chemical element.

hero.hook: Water up to your chin. The fruits above the head. And never a sip, never a bite.

blocks.text: **Tantalum** embodies punished excess. Invited to the table of the gods, this privileged king dares to challenge them. His punishment is refined: having before his eyes what he desires, without ever being able to grasp it.
The myth has crossed language, psychology and even chemistry. “Suffering the torture of Tantalus” is still the name of absolute frustration today.

sections.title: A king too close to the gods

blocks.text: Tantalus is king of Lydia, in Asia Minor. Son of **Zeus** and a nymph, he sometimes shares nectar and ambrosia on Olympus. This familiarity makes him arrogant. He first steals divine foods to offer them to other mortals.

Then comes the horror. To test whether the gods really see everything, he invites the pantheon to a banquet. He kills his own son, **Pelops**, cuts him up and serves him as a dish. The gods retreat. Only **Demeter**, goddess of the harvest, distracted by the grief of her daughter , bites a piece of her shoulder. [[Persephone]]
Zeus resurrects Pelops. The eaten shoulder is replaced by a piece of . Tantalus' lineage, the **Atrides**, will remain cursed: Agamemnon and Orestes will inherit it. [[ivory]]

In the [[Tartarus]], a prison deep beneath the world, Tantalus' punishment reverses his crime. He has insulted the sacred banquet: he will never eat again. Plunged up to his chin in a lake, he died of thirst.

blocks.caption: Tantalum, surrounded by water and inaccessible fruits.

blocks.text: As soon as he tilts his head, the water sinks into the ground. Above, branches bend under figs, pears, pomegranates. As soon as he extends his hand, a wind blows them away. It's not the absence that tortures: it's the deceptive proximity.
A variation adds a third danger: a huge rock hanging above his head, ready to collapse. No rest, even without hunger.

sections.title: From myth to the periodic table

blocks.text: In **1802**, the Swedish chemist **Anders Ekeberg** discovered a metal. He named it **tantalum** (atomic number **73**): immersed in acids, this metal absorbs almost none. Like the thirsty king in the middle of the lake.

blocks.caption: Tantalum, element 73, named after the myth.

blocks.text: Today, the [[chemical element tantalum (Ta, 73)]] is strategic: smartphone capacitors, corrosion-resistant prostheses. In English, *to tantalize* means to excite desire by keeping the object out of reach. In French, “the torture of Tantalus” remains the reference expression.
refers to any situation where the goal seems within reach, but then moves away at the last moment. [[The “torture of Tantalus” as an archetype]]

In psychology, Tantalus illustrates a desire that never goes out: the closer the object, the more burning the failure. In politics, the image is used for promises that fade away as soon as we approach them.
His crime was not just murder. It was an attempt to deceive the gods. In return, it is his own senses that deceive him for eternity: seeing water, seeing fruit, and having nothing.

**Tantalus**, king of Lydia, serves his son **Pelops** to the gods. Condemned to Tartarus, he has water and fruit before his eyes without ever reaching them. His name still lives in the language and in the element **73**.
